c0048: Store properly (cold 41 °F or below, frozen 0 °F or below, dry goods) and label with product and date; ready-to-eat food keeps 7 days max at 41 °F, prep day = day 1 (FDA Food Code 3-501.17). Shelf life by family is in the table at the bottom of this sheet
c0049: Make base sauces, stocks and reductions
c0050: Prep marinades, rubs and soaks that need time
c0051: Make doughs, tart shells and desserts that need to rest
c0052: Do the pre-cooking: confit, braises, sous-vide. Cool anything made ahead in shallow pans, an ice bath or the blast chiller: 135 °F to 70 °F within 2 h, then to 41 °F within 4 h more (FDA Food Code 3-501.14), and log it
c0053: Cut and portion proteins per the recipe card
c0054: Fish served raw or undercooked (ceviche, tartare, marinated, cold-smoked) — parasite destruction: get the supplier's freezing record (−4 °F or below for 7 days, or −31 °F or below until solid + 15 h; FDA Food Code 3-402.11) or freeze it yourself, keep the record 90 days and note the lot
c0055: Prep sides and vegetables: wash, cut and blanch. Wash under running potable water (FDA Food Code 3-302.15); if you use a produce wash or chlorine, only one made for fruits and vegetables, at the label dose, and RINSE well afterwards
c0056: Label everything with product, date, lot and allergens (the 9 major US allergens); ready-to-eat food keeps 7 days max at 41 °F, prep day = day 1

c0059: Check the walk-ins ran all night and log the temperatures (cooler 41 °F or below, freezer 0 °F or below) — log reading: ____ °F. If out of range, don't load the product until it's been assessed
c0060: Finish the final preparations: bake, grill, fry
c0063: Build presentation platters and edible centerpieces
c0065: Pack in labeled hotel pans and insulated food carriers (cambros)
c0066: Check temperatures before loading: hot food 135 °F or above, cold food 41 °F or below — log reading: ____ °F (if you have the HACCP Food Safety Kit Pro, log it on its temperature sheet; if not, in the "Notes" column)
c0067: Check the packed utensils, smallwares and service equipment
c0068: Log the day's production waste (product, quantity and reason): it is the data that corrects the costing for the next event
c0069: Clean and sanitize the production area after loading
c0077: Raw red meat and poultry, whole cuts
c0079: Portion BEFORE freezing: never thaw and refreeze
c0082: More exposed surface: it goes rancid and oxidizes much sooner than a whole cut
c0085: Parasite destruction (−4 °F for 7 days, FDA Food Code 3-402.11) does not replace this shelf life: they are counted separately
c0089: House stocks, sauces, creams and reductions
c0090: Label with the production date AND the freezing date: shelf life counts from the freezing date
c0091: Raw dough, tart shells and puff pastry
c0093: Yeast loses strength: the dough rises poorly afterwards even if it is still safe
c0096: It loses texture before it loses safety; refresh it in the oven, never in the microwave
c0099: Only the ones that freeze well: anything with mayonnaise, gelatin or whipped cream does NOT freeze
c0102: Blanch before freezing: unblanched, it loses color and texture within a few weeks
c0103: Product that has already gone out to service
c0105: Food that has been out on the buffet or has broken the cold chain does not go back in the freezer: toss it

Anything traveling without temperature control goes under time as a public health control (FDA Food Code 3-501.19, written procedure required): mark the time it left 41 °F / 135 °F; the 4 h include the trip AND the service at the venue, and whatever is left at 4 h is discarded

c0144: Check the visual condition of the food after transport
c0145: Log the product temperature at unloading: hot 135 °F or above, cold 41 °F or below — log reading: ____ °F (if you have the HACCP Food Safety Kit Pro, log it on its temperature sheet; if not, in the "Notes" column)

c0550: ▸ This is not a cash count: a catering business has no counter or POS shift. It gets paid per event, almost always by check, ACH (bank transfer) or card, so what to watch is the outstanding BALANCE and its due date, not the drawer over/short.
c0551: How to Use — Before the Event
c0552: ▸ Go through it with the calendar in hand: the "When" column counts DAYS before the event (By 15 days out, By 7 days out, By 3 days out, Day before: deadlines), not hours. Nothing leaves here without a quote accepted in writing and the deposit collected and logged.
c0553: How to Use — After the Event
c0554: ▸ The days that follow (event day, day after, 7 days after, 30 days after): actual count vs. guaranteed count, extras used, invoice sent, balance communicated, payment logged and reconciled with the bank.
c0556: ▸ Fill in only the GREEN cells: quote and extras BEFORE sales tax, how that base splits between "Taxable subtotal" and "Non-taxable subtotal", the deposit already collected, what was paid after the event and the balance due date. The total, the sales tax, the balance, the amount outstanding and the STATUS are formulas. The sales tax comes from the rate in cell C3 of the "Event Billing Log".
c0557: ▸ What carries sales tax is decided by your state (check with your CPA or the department of revenue): in many states food, drinks, rentals and the mandatory service charge. A mandatory service charge is NOT a tip: it is your revenue, and whatever part of it you pay to staff is wages on payroll for the IRS, not tips (Rev. Rul. 2012-18). Some states (e.g., NY, MA) presume an undisclosed service charge belongs to staff: state your policy in the contract. The gratuity is the client's choice, goes on a separate line and belongs to the team. A tax-exempt client needs their exemption certificate on file. If the two subtotals don't add up to quote + extras, the sheet warns you.
c0558: ▸ BALANCE DUE turns AMBER while any balance remains, and the STATUS changes to "OVERDUE" only once the due date has passed: it is the signal to chase the payment.
c0559: ▸ If the event had a bar with CASH payment, count the money in the optional table at the bottom (denominations, minus the starting bank) and, if you like, add that net cash to "Paid after the event" yourself. It is not linked on purpose: most events have no cash, and a fixed formula would leave a 0 subtracting where it shouldn't. The cash table has US bills and coins ($100 … 1¢; a "25¢ roll" counts $10 and a "10¢ roll" $5); in the UK, Canada or Australia, unprotect the sheet (no password) and change each row's label and the multiplier in its Subtotal formula.
c0560: ▸ One row per event: at a glance you see how much was invoiced, which deposits came in, what is pending and how many events are OVERDUE. The TOTALS row adds up the year and counts the pending ones.
c0561: ▸ Everything you fill in is GREEN: Assigned to, When, ✓ Done, Initials, the settlement amounts and the Event Billing Log rows.
